lessons.title: PE: price versus profit
lessons.plain_english: PE is roughly how many rupees investors pay for one rupee of annual profit. A high PE means large expectations are already in the price; a low PE may be cheap or may reflect a weakening business.
lessons.decision_rule: Compare PE with growth quality, forecast resilience and peers. Never treat low PE as sufficient evidence by itself.
lessons.example: A PE of 12 with shrinking profits can be less attractive than a PE of 20 with durable, well-priced growth.
lessons.check_question: Why can the lowest-PE stock still be a weak choice?
lessons.check_answer: Its earnings or business quality may be deteriorating, making the apparent cheapness a value trap.

lessons.title: PEG: what you pay for growth
lessons.plain_english: PEG relates a company's PE to its expected growth. Below 1 can signal attractively priced growth, around 1 can be reasonable, and well above 1 suggests optimism is expensive.
lessons.decision_rule: Use PEG as a comparison tool, then confirm that the growth forecast and business quality are credible.
lessons.example: Two companies may grow at similar rates, but the one with a much lower PEG asks you to pay less for each unit of expected growth.
lessons.check_question: Does PEG below 1 guarantee a good return?
lessons.check_answer: No. It is useful evidence, but forecasts can fail and business risk still matters.

lessons.title: Sharpe: return earned efficiently
lessons.plain_english: Sharpe asks how much return a portfolio earned for the bumpiness it endured. Higher is generally better when calculations use comparable periods and assumptions.
lessons.decision_rule: Do not chase a little extra expected return when it requires a disproportionate increase in risk.
lessons.example: An 18% return with moderate volatility may represent better decision quality than 21% with extreme volatility.
lessons.check_question: What does a higher Sharpe ratio reward?
lessons.check_answer: More excess return per unit of measured volatility.

lessons.title: Drawdown: the fall you must survive
lessons.plain_english: Maximum drawdown is the worst fall from a previous high. It shows the loss an investor would have had to endure before recovery.
lessons.decision_rule: Compare end returns with the depth and duration of losses along the way.
lessons.example: After a 50% fall, a portfolio needs a 100% gain merely to return to its old peak.
lessons.check_question: Why is a deep drawdown especially costly?
lessons.check_answer: Recovery requires a proportionally larger gain and may test the investor's ability to remain invested.

lessons.title: Diversification: different risks, not just more names
lessons.plain_english: Diversification reduces dependence on one company, sector or economic force. Owning many highly correlated stocks may still amount to one concentrated bet.
lessons.decision_rule: Check weights, sectors and shared risk drivers—not merely ticker count.
lessons.example: Ten lenders may respond similarly to a credit shock, while a smaller set spanning distinct drivers may diversify better.
lessons.check_question: Why can twelve stocks still be concentrated?
lessons.check_answer: They may share the same sector or economic exposure and therefore fall together.

lessons.title: Rebalancing: restore each holding's role
lessons.plain_english: Rebalancing changes holdings when prices, forecasts, risk or portfolio weights change. A trim need not mean a company is bad; it can mean its role became too large.
lessons.decision_rule: Sell first, then direct monthly capital and proceeds toward the strongest feasible whole-share portfolio.
lessons.example: A winner at 40% of the portfolio can be trimmed to fund several attractive holdings and reduce one-company risk.
lessons.check_question: Why might you trim a healthy company?
lessons.check_answer: Its position may be too large or other opportunities may now improve the portfolio's return-risk balance.

lessons.title: VaR and expected shortfall: look into the tail
lessons.plain_english: VaR estimates a loss threshold for a chosen confidence level. Expected shortfall estimates the average loss in the worse cases beyond that threshold.
lessons.decision_rule: Use both as scenario-aware risk estimates, never as guarantees or maximum-loss limits.
lessons.example: A 95% monthly VaR of ₹18,000 means the model expects roughly one month in twenty to be worse; expected shortfall describes those worse months.
lessons.check_question: What does VaR not tell you?
lessons.check_answer: It does not cap the loss or fully describe how severe losses beyond the threshold can become.

lessons.title: Good decision, bad month
lessons.plain_english: Decision quality uses evidence available before the outcome. A disciplined portfolio can suffer a bad month; a reckless portfolio can get lucky.
lessons.decision_rule: Judge the move first on valuation, expected return, downside and diversification; show the subsequent market outcome separately.
lessons.example: A diversified portfolio may fall in a broad shock and still deserve an excellent process score.
lessons.check_question: Why should one-month return not own the BTI score?
lessons.check_answer: Because the return includes luck and information that was unknowable when the move was made.
